<reason>The motion's comparator is employer-based systems "that tie access to work status." PRO anchored the whole debate on that text and showed that every counter-model CON offered (Germany, Japan, Netherlands) severs access from work status by law; CON's own words in [B2.6] ("well-designed employer systems never ask her to" job-shop) and especially [B4.1] ("what German law unties is continuity, not financing") effectively concede that the tie the motion condemns is indefensible, and PRO exploited both cleanly in its closing. CON's unfalsifiability charge was a fair complaint about the motion's construction but functionally swapped in a different question (single-payer vs. employer-routed universal systems), which the judging frame says not to reward. On the residual one-payer-vs-many-funds comparison CON did real work (austerity exposure, queue plus private top-up relocating bank-balance rationing, exit through fund-switching), and PRO's answers there were adequate but not decisive; PRO also lost its final sentence to clipping. Net: PRO won the decisive definitional clash on the motion as written, CON was competitive on the narrower comparison, giving PRO a clear but not commanding win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A2.1]-[A2.2] turn ("That is not a rebuttal of the motion. That is the motion.") reframing CON's Germany/Japan/Netherlands examples as concessions, later sealed by PRO's closing reading of CON's own [B4.1] admission that German law "unties continuity" — continuity being access.</best_rebuttal>
